cheatsheet:
**Opening**
`FILE *f = fopen("log.txt", "r");` · modes `"r"` read, `"w"` write (wipes), `"a"` append · `if (f == NULL) { ... }`

**Reading**
`while (fgets(line, sizeof line, f) != NULL)` · `fscanf(f, "%d", &x)` · then `fclose(f);`

**Writing**
`fprintf(f, "speed %d\n", speed);`

**Errors**
Calls return failure (NULL, EOF, fewer values). `strerror(errno)` says why; `perror("name")` prints it to stderr.

**Parsing lines**
`if (sscanf(line, "%31s %d", name, &age) == 2)` · scanf/sscanf return how many values they filled

lessons.title: Files: open, write, read, close
lessons.concept:
A file is opened with `FILE *f = fopen("flight.log", "w");`. The mode says what you'll do: `"r"` read, `"w"` write (wipes the file first), `"a"` add to the end.

Writing is `fprintf(f, ...)`, exactly like printf with the file in front. Reading a line is `fgets(line, sizeof line, f)`, which returns `NULL` when there's nothing left, so it makes a perfect loop condition.

`fopen` returns `NULL` when it can't open the file. Always check, and `fclose(f)` when you're done.

drills.prompt: Fill the blanks to print every line of `cargo.txt` (the mode goes in with its quotes).
drills.explain: Open for reading with `"r"`, read line by line with `fgets` until it returns NULL, then `fclose`.

drills.prompt: This numbers the lines of `cargo.txt`, but the last line always shows up twice. Fix the loop.
drills.explain: `feof` only turns true **after** a read has already failed. So the loop runs once more, fgets fails and leaves the old line in the buffer, and it's printed again. Loop on fgets itself.

drills.prompt: Print how many lines `log.txt` has. (Every line ends with a newline.)

files.log.txt:
boot ok
fans on
all good

drills.explain: Each successful fgets is one line. Note the empty line in the last test still counts: it's just `\n`.

lessons.title: When things go wrong
lessons.concept:
In C nothing throws an error at you: functions **return** a sign that they failed, and it's on you to look. fopen returns `NULL`; scanf returns how many values it managed to read.

When a library call fails it also sets `errno` (from `<errno.h>`) to a code saying why. `strerror(errno)` (from `<string.h>`) turns it into words like *No such file or directory*.

`perror("main.log")` prints the same thing to **stderr**, a second output stream meant for errors. The judge only compares stdout, so use printf when the message is part of the expected output.

predict.answer:
can't open main.log: No such file or directory

predict.explain: main.log doesn't exist, so the first open fails and says why; the backup it wrote a moment ago opens fine.

drills.prompt: `perror("log.txt")` prints `log.txt: No such file or directory`. Where does it go?
options: To stderr, a separate stream, so the judge's output check never sees it
drills.answer: To stderr, a separate stream, so the judge's output check never sees it
drills.explain: stderr is for error messages: you see them in the run results, but they never mix into the output being checked.

drills.prompt: What does fopen give back when the file isn't there?
drills.explain: Using that NULL in fgets or fscanf crashes the program, which is why every fopen gets an `if (f == NULL)`.

drills.prompt: Read the fuel level from `fuel.txt` and print `fuel N`. If the file is missing **or** doesn't start with a number, print `fuel unknown`. Right now a missing file crashes it.
drills.explain: Two checks: fopen's NULL for the missing file, and fscanf's return value (1 means it read one number) for a file with junk in it.

drills.prompt:
The input is words separated by spaces. Some are whole numbers, some aren't. Add up the numbers and count the rest, then print `sum S, bad B`.

Use scanf's return value: `1` means it read a number, `0` means the next word isn't one (skip it with `scanf("%*s")`), `EOF` means the input is finished.
drills.explain: When scanf returns 0 it hasn't moved past the bad word, so without the `%*s` skip it would fail on the same word forever.

lessons.title: Reading records safely
lessons.concept:
Real files have broken lines. The safe pattern is: read a whole line with `fgets`, then pick it apart with `sscanf`, which is scanf reading from a string.

sscanf returns how many values it filled. For `"%31s %d"` that's 2 when the line is good; anything less means skip it. (`%31s` stops a long word from overflowing a 32-char array.)

Because you already have the whole line, a bad one can't knock the rest of the file out of step.

drills.prompt: `tanks.txt` starts with a header line `tank litres`, then one tank per line, like `A 120`. Print `total T`, the litres added up.

files.tanks.txt:
tank litres
MAIN 500
AUX 250
R1 255

drills.explain: The header gives sscanf a word but no number, so `== 2` skips it for free. (Reading and throwing away the first line works too.)

drills.prompt: This averages the crew's ages from `crew.txt`, but a broken line sneaks into the count. Fix the check.
drills.explain: A broken line still fills the name, so sscanf returns 1, which counts as true. The line is good only when it returns exactly 2.

checkpoint.prompt: Which mode wipes the file and starts it fresh?
checkpoint.explain: `"w"` truncates; `"a"` keeps the old contents and adds to the end.

checkpoint.prompt: Why loop on `fgets(...) != NULL` instead of `while (!feof(f))`?
options: feof only turns true after a read has already failed, so the last line repeats
feof doesn't work on text files
fgets closes the file for you
checkpoint.answer: feof only turns true after a read has already failed, so the last line repeats
checkpoint.explain: Let the read itself tell you it's done.
The comma in the format matches the comma in the text, so both numbers are filled.

checkpoint.prompt: fopen just returned NULL. Which line prints **why**, as words, to stdout?
checkpoint.explain: errno holds a code; strerror turns it into a message (and perror would send it to stderr instead).

checkpoint.prompt: What do you do with every `FILE *` you opened, once you're done with it?
checkpoint.explain: fclose flushes anything still waiting to be written and releases the file.
